Abstract

  1. Glucocorticoid differences between dominant and subordinate animals take many forms: subordinates are higher in some species, dominants in others, top-ranked individuals are sometimes exceptions, and many studies find no rank effect. Reviews invoke social and ecological moderators, but no mechanistic model lets both the hierarchy and the physiological burden emerge from the same local decisions.
  2. We built a bounded-rational network game in which initially identical individuals forage, contest food patches and mates, yield, escape and affiliate according to their own experience-based beliefs. Each individual carries a fast activation and a slow allostatic load, driven only by realized events: defeat, intimidation, effort, energy deficit and unpredictability. Rank is computed by the analyst and never enters any behavioural or physiological equation. Analytic properties were verified symbolically and by machine-checked proofs.
  3. Linear hierarchies required resource-holding feedback, in which energetic condition affects contest success, and formed reliably only in conjunction with food scarcity, low choice noise and long memory. Purely dyadic belief dynamics never produced a linear order.
  4. Where hierarchies formed, predeclared rules distinguished four profiles of load across rank: a graded rise towards the bottom (scarce, monopolizable food), a step (no escape, or mating competition), a peak among contenders at ranks 2–3 below a low-load alpha (rich, contestable food without scarcity) and a middle peak (a guarded breeding monopoly). Rank thirds read the contender peak as an inverted U in groups of 6 but dominant-high in groups of 10–20. Subordinate-high profiles held at group size 20. The model never produced a confirmed high-load alpha or a rise in load after instability.
  5. These outputs reproduce subordinate-high glucocorticoids under despotism and constraint, low glucocorticoids in alpha female baboons, and costs of contested positions near the top; they partly reproduce dominant-high patterns, but not the high-glucocorticoid alpha males of baboons and macaques. The model predicts that dominant-high gradients are carried by challengers rather than alphas, and that seasonal mating competition reshapes rather than reverses gradients; identifying mechanisms requires full rank profiles, not correlations or rank thirds. The misses point to two missing ingredients: costs borne only by the top position, and an input from rank insecurity.

Keywords: agent-based model, allostatic load, bounded rationality, dominance hierarchy, game theory, glucocorticoids, social rank, social stress

Introduction

Social rank is one of the most studied correlates of physiological stress in animals, yet the direction of the relationship is not consistent. In stable, despotic primate hierarchies, subordinates often have higher basal glucocorticoids (Sapolsky 2005; Abbott et al. 2003), as do subordinate female mice in complex groups (Williamson et al. 2019). In many cooperative breeders dominants are higher (Creel 2001; Creel et al. 1997), as are high-ranking male chimpanzees in some communities (Muller and Wrangham 2004; Muller et al. 2021). In Amboseli baboons, glucocorticoids rise with declining rank among males ranked two to eight, but the alpha male is an exception, with values like those of low-ranking males (Gesquiere et al. 2011, 2025). Elsewhere, rank and glucocorticoids are unrelated (Stavisky et al. 2001; Preis et al. 2019; Edwards et al. 2020; Van der Weyde et al. 2016). Comparative analyses converge on a conditional explanation: the individual with the greater relative allostatic burden has the higher glucocorticoids, whichever rank that is (Goymann and Wingfield 2004). Subordinates pay more where hierarchies are despotic, food is monopolizable, harassment is frequent and escape or support is lacking. Dominants pay more where status must be actively defended or reproduction monopolized (Sapolsky 2005; Abbott et al. 2003; Creel 2001).

This explanation is verbal. It names moderators (resource distribution, escape, support, stability, reproductive skew) without showing how a given combination produces a given rank profile. Existing models address the two halves of the problem separately. Winner–loser and self-reinforcement models explain how hierarchies emerge from repeated contests (Dugatkin 1997; Hemelrijk 1999; Chase et al. 2002; van Haeringen and Hemelrijk 2022), and reinforcement-learning models explain how dominance behaviour evolves (Leimar 2021). Reproductive-skew games assign different costs to dominants and subordinates (Rubenstein and Shen 2009; Rubenstein 2007), and network approaches separate status from status certainty (Vandeleest et al. 2016). None of these lets the hierarchy and the physiological burden of each position emerge together from the same decisions. As a result, none can ask which rank–stress profiles a self-organizing hierarchy can generate at all, and which field patterns would need additional mechanisms.

Answering that question imposes two constraints. First, rank must be an output, not an input: if load depends on rank, any rank–load pattern can be produced by assumption. Second, the physiological variable must integrate the events an individual actually experiences, with the same contest never counted twice. Allostatic load (McEwen and Wingfield 2003) provides such a variable. We treat it as a dimensionless burden, not as a glucocorticoid concentration, because hormone levels can rise, fall or stay unchanged under chronic challenge (Dickens and Romero 2013; MacDougall-Shackleton et al. 2019).

We built a model under these constraints and used it to ask three questions. When does a linear dominance hierarchy emerge from local, experience-based decisions? Where it does, what shapes does the profile of load across rank take: monotone increasing or decreasing, U-shaped, inverted U, flat, or with an exceptional alpha? And which of the patterns reported in wild and captive animals can the model reproduce, under which conditions, and which can it not?

Materials and methods

Here we follow the overview elements of the ODD protocol (Grimm et al. 2020); the full description, with every parameter, is in Appendix S1. Figure 1 summarizes the model.

Model overview

Individuals and state. A group of \(N\) individuals (6–20) starts exchangeable. No rank is assigned and no physiological parameter is linked to status. Each individual \(i\) has an energy reserve \(E_i \in [0,1]\), a fast activation \(z_i \ge 0\), a slow load \(A_i \ge 0\), a received-support trace, a mode (forage, rest, withdrawn, holding a food patch, consorting) and private beliefs. Time is continuous; each individual receives decision opportunities as a Poisson process of rate 1, so total activity scales with \(N\) rather than \(N^2\).

Ecology and energy. Dispersed food is available to every forager at rate \(g_s\). A fixed number \(K_F\) of food patches yield \(\rho_c g_s\) to a single holder. Optional mating seasons add \(K_M\) consortship assets. Every mode has a basal cost; scarcity is set by the ratio of maintenance cost to dispersed intake (\(m/g_s\)). A conserved energy ledger records intake, maintenance, effort, injury, surplus and deficit. Unpaid maintenance is recorded as a deficit, never silently clipped, and the ledger identity is checked after every event.

Actions. At an opportunity, an individual meets up to two others and sees up to two assets. It may forage, rest, withdraw to a refuge, keep or occupy an asset, challenge a holder, aggress without a stake, or propose grooming or cooperation, choosing low or high effort for contests. A challenged or aggressed individual submits, attempts escape (succeeding with probability \(\phi\)) or fights. Positive interactions need the partner’s acceptance. Fights are decided by a Tullock contest success function (Skaperdas 1996), \[P_{ij} = \sigma\!\left(\theta \ln\frac{e_i}{e_j} + \zeta \ln\frac{\varepsilon_c + E_i}{\varepsilon_c + E_j}\right),\] where \(e\) is effort and \(\zeta\) sets how strongly energetic condition affects outcomes. With \(\zeta > 0\), winning patches raises \(E\) and so later win probability: a resource-holding feedback that is earned ecologically, but is a per-individual scalar and is reported as such.

Beliefs. Individuals hold only their own decaying evidence (rate \(\gamma\)): wins, losses, yields given and received, partners’ responses and efforts, acceptance of proposals, and the rate at which their holdings are challenged. Win forecasts are Beta posterior means for each partner; a dyad with no evidence is unknown, not equal. Two optional, separately ablated mechanisms couple beliefs across dyads. A standing cue sets the prior for every partner from the individual’s own share of fights won and yields received over all partners; its influence fades as dyadic evidence accumulates. Bystander learning adds discounted pseudo-counts from observed fights. Individuals never observe others’ energy, activation, load or rank.

Decisions. Each option is valued by its expected utility of food (weighted by a concave, state-dependent value of energy), mating, injury, received safety events (attacks that end badly for the recipient, valued at \(s_S\)) and grooming, over a horizon \(H\) discounted by the learned hazard of losing a holding. There is no rank term and no load term. The primary policy (P2) chooses by softmax over options with temperature \(\tau_T\) relative to a reference utility. Responses use the same rule. A long-horizon variant (P3-T) and a policy that adds a learned linear critic of the individual’s own state (temporal-difference learning, no actor update; Sutton and Barto (2018)) were also run.

Physiology. Activation and load follow \[\dot z_i = -\lambda_z z_i + u_i(t), \qquad \dot A_i = k\,z_i - \delta_A (A_i - \bar A),\] with instantaneous jumps \(z_i \to z_i + q\) at events. Inputs come from an auditable exposure ledger, and each contest enters exactly once:

  • jumps: defeat (\(q_D\)), intimidation on yielding (\(q_S\)), injury (\(q_I\)), contest effort for both fighters (\(q_E e\), the cost-of-dominance pathway), escape effort (\(q_{\mathrm{esc}}\)), and the surprise of negative outcomes relative to the individual’s own forecast;
  • continuous inputs: activity effort and energy deficit.

Support can either buffer threat inputs or speed recovery; the two are tested separately and never subtract load directly. With \(\lambda_z = 1 \gg \delta_A = 0.01\), load integrates activation over about 100 decision intervals. Physiology does not feed back into behaviour (one-way coupling) except in the two-way coupling experiments below.

Implementation and verification (Appendix S2). The model is a discrete-event simulation in Julia (Bezanson et al. 2017), with one independent random stream for each purpose, so results do not depend on parallel execution order. Between events, physiology is advanced by its closed-form flow map. Verification ran on three levels:

  • Symbolic: fixed points, single-pulse responses, the timing-independence of mean load under repeated jumps, and the decision formulas were derived in SymPy (Meurer et al. 2017). The Julia decision code is generated from these derivations and checked against them.
  • Formal: nonnegativity of \(z\) and \(A\) without clipping, the closed-form solution and its uniqueness, energy conservation, bounds on forecasts, properties of the contest function and the bounds of an optional reserve variable were proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib (The mathlib Community 2020).
  • Numerical: the simulator passes 13,744 automated tests, including comparison with an independent ODE solver.

Analysis

All analysis is done outside the simulation, from the event log, under frozen analysis plans written before the sweeps they govern.

Windows and structure. Each run lasts 3,000 time units. After a burn-in of 1,000, four windows of 500 are analysed, and each of the first three is classified using the next for persistence and prediction. Dominance evidence pools fight outcomes with submissions and escapes. A window is Linear when all four of the following hold:

  • Landau’s \(h' \ge 0.8\) (de Vries 1995);
  • triangle transitivity exceeds an orientation null at \(p < 0.05\) (Shizuka and McDonald 2012);
  • at least 80% of dyads are observed;
  • a linear (Bradley–Terry) order predicts the next window’s outcomes as well as dyad-specific history does.

Ranks for all later analyses are David’s scores (David 1987).

Near-linear windows are transitive, consistent and persistent with \(h' \ge 0.6\). Other classes are nontransitive, egalitarian, unstable and degenerate. The group, not the individual, is the unit of replication: each parameter point has 20–40 independent groups.

Rank–load profile shapes. For each group we take its first Linear or near-linear window. In that window we standardize window-mean excess load (\(A - \bar A\)) across the group’s members and order individuals by David’s score (position 1 = top). The positions are split into top, middle and bottom thirds, with means \(T\), \(M\) and \(B\). Three contrasts are bootstrapped over groups (2,000 resamples, 95% intervals): \(\Delta_1 = M - T\), \(\Delta_2 = B - M\) and \(\Delta_{BT} = B - T\).

  • Signs: a contrast is flat if its interval lies within \(\pm 0.5\) standard deviations, and up or down if its interval excludes zero.
  • Shapes:
    • monotone subordinate-high (both contrasts up or flat, at least one up);
    • monotone dominant-high (the reverse);
    • U-shaped (down, then up);
    • inverted U (up, then down);
    • flat (all three contrasts flat).
  • Alpha modifier: an alpha peak or alpha trough is recorded when the alpha contrast \(\alpha_c = \ell_{(1)} - (\ell_{(2)} + \ell_{(3)})/2\) has an interval entirely above \(0.5\) or below \(-0.5\).

This rule was declared, and amended once (to make “flat” attainable at the planned replication), before any run that it classifies. Mean activation \(z\) was classified in the same way as an acute analogue.

Because thirds contain different ranks at different group sizes, we also report a contender contrast, \(\kappa = (\ell_{(2)} + \ell_{(3)})/2 - \mathrm{mean}(\ell_{(5)}, \dots, \ell_{(N)})\), which compares ranks 2–3 with ranks 5 and below on the same profile. It was defined after an exploratory scan at \(N = 20\) and tested on new seeds (Appendix S4).

Experiments

Earlier experiments (more than 12,000 runs over factorial designs of condition dependence, belief coupling, noise, memory, scarcity and group size) mapped where hierarchies emerge and how the top-versus-bottom load gap divides among input channels. We assessed global sensitivity with Morris screening and Sobol indices (Morris 1991; Saltelli et al. 2010). We re-tested headline claims at four base points, and tested two-way coupling one mechanism at a time: load-dependent effort capacity, load-slowed recovery, and a depletable functional reserve.

For profile shapes we ran two sets of simulations.

  • Shape scan: a re-run of the robustness designs at bases A, B and C (111 parameter points × 20 groups). Each design varies the number of food patches and escape, patch richness and contest cost, channel ablations, support, and coupling. The re-run reproduced every previously recorded output bit for bit, confirming that the added profile records did not alter the simulations.
  • Wildlife scenarios: 17 scenarios (40 groups each), each translating a social–ecological condition reported in the field into model settings, with predictions fixed in advance (Table 2).
  • Confirmation run: one exploratory finding was re-tested on independent seeds.
  • Group size: the scenarios were repeated at \(N = 20\) (40 groups each, windows three times longer), with matched \(N = 10\) controls, under predictions fixed in advance. A second confirmation run tested the contender contrast on new seeds (Appendix S4).

Results

Linear hierarchies emerge only through conjunctions of conditions

Under the primary policy, linear hierarchies were rare at default settings. Across 576 parameter points at \(N = 6\) and 10 (11,680 runs), 28 points produced Linear structure in at least half of their groups, and every one had \(\zeta = 2\) (Figure 2). Purely dyadic belief dynamics (\(\zeta = 0\), no standing cue, no bystander learning) produced at most 2 of 20 Linear groups at any point. Instead they produced stable, asymmetric dyads that did not compose into a transitive order.

The standing cue and bystander learning raised the rate only in combination with condition dependence. The best \(N = 10\) setting (base A: scarcity, low noise, cue and bystanders) was Linear in 18 of 20 groups.

Global sensitivity analysis showed that structure was interaction-dominated, with first-order Sobol indices near zero and total indices of 0.26–0.71. Belief decay, the safety value, escape, scarcity, contest cost, patch number, choice noise and patch richness all mattered jointly.

High escape success (\(\phi \ge 0.8\)) abolished order rather than gradually weakening the load gradient. Closed groups of 20 did not order at base A. Fast fission–fusion into short-lived subgroups restored Linear hierarchies at \(N = 20\) (13–17 of 20 groups).

Load gradients follow exposure channels and ecology

Where hierarchies formed under scarcity, load was usually higher in subordinates: 103 of 119 classifiable points in the base-A maps (Figure 3). Channel attribution decomposes the top-versus-bottom gap exactly into input channels, and ablating a channel shifts the gap by its share. The gap was carried by energy deficit (subordinates excluded from patches) and defeat. With many patches, intimidation carried it. At a single rich patch, contest effort paid by dominants nearly offset subordinates’ deficit.

Without scarcity, the same mechanisms gave dominant-high gradients. Support by threat buffering removed the defeat share, whereas recovery facilitation shrank the whole gap.

Two-way coupling mechanisms had distinct signatures:

  • Load-slowed recovery amplified gaps 4- to 11-fold without changing behaviour.
  • Load-limited effort capacity and a depletable reserve were stabilizing: loaded individuals yielded rather than escalated, and gaps shrank. Strong reserve depletion reduced Linear groups from 19 to 3 of 20.

Four profiles of load across rank

The shape rule resolved profiles that a correlation coefficient conflates (Figure 4; Table 2).

  • Graded subordinate-high profile. Across the base-A scan, 25 of 28 evaluable points showed it, with load rising steadily from top to bottom (scenario W0: \(\Delta_{BT} = 2.01\), 95% interval 1.96–2.06).
  • Step. Removing escape (W1) or adding a year-round mating monopoly (W5a) produced one: the top three individuals were low and everyone below was about equally high. In W5a and W7 it came with an alpha trough (W5a: \(\alpha_c = -0.92\), −1.07 to −0.78).
  • Contender peak below a low-load alpha. Ranks 2–3 carried the most load, the alpha little, and everyone below was near the group mean. It appeared without scarcity where several rich patches could be contested. It was common at base B: \(\kappa > 0.9\) at all 19 scan points with three patches of richness \(\rho_c \ge 4\) (W3b: \(\kappa = 1.53\), 1.36–1.69). It also appeared with ample food at base A (W3a: 1.30, 0.95–1.63) and with tolerant contests (W9b: 0.89, 0.37–1.36), although few groups were ordered in those two conditions (7–9 of 40).
  • Middle peak. Ample food combined with a guarded breeding monopoly (W4) produced it, with the highest loads at ranks 3–6 (\(\Delta_1 = 1.02\); \(\Delta_2 = -0.52\); \(\kappa = -0.29\)). It needed a closed group: with fast fission–fusion the same settings gave a subordinate-high profile with an alpha trough.

The contender peak is one profile that the thirds rule labels differently by group size. At \(N = 6\), rank 3 lies in the middle third, so the rule reads an inverted U (W3b: \(\Delta_1 = 0.47\), 0.27 to 0.65; \(\Delta_2 = -0.99\), −1.18 to −0.82). At \(N = 10\) and 20, ranks 2–3 share the top third with the alpha, so it reads dominant-high, the label given to W9b. The frozen correlation-based classes fared worse: of the 24 inverted-U points, 9 had been classed dominant-high, 6 subordinate-high, 7 indeterminate and 2 weak/null. Shapes based on acute activation \(z\) agreed with those based on load at 80 of 84 points.

Three shapes did not appear as distinct profiles.

  • Flat: no evaluable point at \(N = 6\) or 10 was flat. The one flat classification, at \(N = 20\), had a strong contender peak that the thirds averaged away (\(\kappa = 1.45\)).
  • U: one point only.
  • Alpha peak: one exploratory scan point (base B, a single rich patch with easy escape) had the alpha carrying the most load (\(\alpha_c = 1.37\), 0.55–2.09; 9 groups). On independent seeds with 40 groups the direction replicated, but the interval (1.17, 0.44–1.80) fell below the declared threshold, so the alpha-exception was not confirmed. A long-horizon planner holding a single rich patch (W5b) placed the alpha above ranks 2–3 (\(\alpha_c = 0.58\), 0.34–0.79) but still below the bottom half of the group.

Profiles at larger group size

Closed groups of 20 did not order at base A (0 of 40 groups), so we tested the scenarios at \(N = 20\) under fast fission–fusion, comparing each with an \(N = 10\) fission–fusion control (Appendix S4, Table S4). Every prediction that could be tested held:

  • Graded rise: with and without escape, the subordinate-high profile was unchanged at \(N = 20\) (40 and 39 of 40 groups ordered; \(\Delta_{BT} = 1.97\) and 1.81, against 2.05 and 2.07 at \(N = 10\); Figure 5, right).
  • Mating monopoly: it again gave subordinate-high load with an alpha trough.
  • Base C: it kept its subordinate-high profile with an alpha trough, though only 6 of 40 groups ordered.

Base B did not order at \(N = 20\), so the inverted U could not be tested there directly. At the nearest settings that did order, base B or C with lower choice noise (\(\tau_T = 0.03\)) and no scarcity, the profile was a contender peak at ranks 2–3 (Figure 5, left). This was confirmed on new seeds, with 31 and 39 of 40 groups ordered: \(\kappa = 1.23\) (0.84–1.62) and 1.45 (1.06–1.79), and \(\alpha_c = -1.53\) and \(-2.13\). The peak therefore stays at the same absolute ranks as groups grow, rather than at the same relative position. The middle peak and the tolerant-contest profile could not be tested at \(N = 20\), because too few groups ordered.

Scenario tests against field patterns

Most predictions fixed before the runs held (Table 2):

  • Despotic, constrained groups (W0–W2) were subordinate-high without an alpha peak, and support shrank the load gap in 40 of 40 paired groups.
  • A mating monopoly with food competition (W5a) was subordinate-high with a low-load alpha.
  • Fission–fusion (W8a, W8b) kept subordinate-high profiles.
  • Seasonal mating raised mean load in season in 40 of 40 groups.
  • Acute activation and load agreed in shape.

Five predictions failed:

  • Removing the alpha did not raise load across the hierarchy. Mean load in the following window was lower than in matched unmanipulated groups in 28 of 40 pairs, and fights did not increase.
  • Seasonal mating did not enlarge the load gap. Instead the profile changed from a graded rise out of season to a step with a low alpha in season, without reversing.
  • Ample food (W3a) was indeterminate rather than dominant-high, with few ordered groups.
  • The long-horizon planner showed no alpha peak in acute activation.
  • Full tolerance ordered 9 of 40 groups rather than fewer than 5, the same rate as earlier runs.

Discussion

A single set of local rules, in which rank never enters behaviour or physiology, generated four distinct profiles of burden across a dominance hierarchy. Which profile appeared was governed by the moderators named in the comparative literature (Sapolsky 2005; Abbott et al. 2003; Goymann and Wingfield 2004): food scarcity and monopolizability, escape, how quickly contests settle, and whether a breeding position must be guarded. The model therefore turns the verbal “relative allostatic load” hypothesis (Goymann and Wingfield 2004) into a mechanism, with no rank-dependent parameters. It shows that the diversity of field patterns is an expected consequence of self-organized exposure rather than noise around a universal rule.

Patterns the model reproduces. Subordinate-high profiles arose wherever scarcity let holders exclude others from patches and escape was limited. These are the conditions under which primate subordinates show high glucocorticoids (Sapolsky 2005; Abbott et al. 2003) and confined or captive subordinates show sustained activation or altered stress-axis regulation (Øverli et al. 1999; Michopoulos et al. 2012; Kohn et al. 2016). Support shrank the gap, consistent with the support moderator in primate comparisons (Abbott et al. 2003).

A distinctly low-load alpha above a nearly flat plateau was common. This matches female baboons, in which alpha status predicts lower glucocorticoids while proportional rank explains little (Levy et al. 2020). In the model it arises because the top individual is yielded to without contest, so it pays neither defeat nor contest effort.

The contender peak matches the finding that baboon males’ cortisol rose with reversals in their dominance relationships with the males immediately below them (Sapolsky 1992). In the model, contests concentrate where outcomes are least settled, among the contenders just below the top, at the same absolute ranks whatever the group size. Where they are not offset by exclusion from food, these contenders carry the most load. The occasional U-shaped profile parallels susceptibility at both the top and the bottom of hierarchies in some rodent studies (Larrieu et al. 2017; LeClair et al. 2021).

Patterns reproduced only in part. Dominant-high gradients, reported in wild dogs, wolves and competitive male chimpanzees (Creel et al. 1997; Mech 1999; Muller and Wrangham 2004; Muller et al. 2021), arose in the model only as the contender peak, read through coarse rank classes. In groups of 10 or more, a top third that contains a low-load alpha and two high-load contenders averages to “dominant-high”. The high-load individuals were the contenders at ranks 2–3, not the alpha.

This yields a testable prediction. Where dominants as a class have higher glucocorticoids, contrasting the alpha with the next two ranks, as has been done in baboons and rhesus macaques (Gesquiere et al. 2011; Milich et al. 2018), should show that the excess belongs to the contenders, unless the top position bears costs that no other position does.

Mating seasons reshaped the profile and raised everyone’s load but did not reverse it. Some field reversals (Kotrschal et al. 1998) may involve parental costs that the model lacks.

Patterns not reproduced, and what they imply. The model did not generate a confirmed high-load alpha: the J-shaped profile of Amboseli males (Gesquiere et al. 2011, 2025) and the mating-season alpha cost in rhesus males (Milich et al. 2018). Mate guarding as modelled added to subordinates’ exclusion and produced the opposite, an alpha trough. The nearest cases (a long-horizon holder of a single rich patch, and one scan setting that failed confirmation) placed the alpha above ranks 2–3 but not reliably above everyone. Both depended on the alpha alone defending an asset. This suggests that the field alpha-exception requires a cost borne only by the top position, such as sustained consortship effort or intervention in others’ conflicts.

Nor did removing the alpha raise load across ranks, as instability does in baboons, chimpanzees and hyenas (Bergman et al. 2005; Preis et al. 2019). In the model the vacancy was filled by the existing order without escalation, and individuals have no physiological input from uncertainty about their own position. Adding a rank-insecurity input, built from each individual’s own forecasts and not from analyst rank, is a natural extension.

Finally, the model never produced a genuinely flat profile within an ordered group; its one flat classification was a contender peak averaged away by thirds. Field nulls (Stavisky et al. 2001; Preis et al. 2019; Edwards et al. 2020) may therefore reflect the absence of a linear order, or small absolute differences that are clear in shape but undetectable against assay noise (as in W3b, where the top-to-bottom gap was 13% of mean load). They need not reflect opposing costs cancelling exactly.

Implications for field studies. Two methodological points follow. First, a correlation coefficient or a coarse high/middle/low contrast cannot distinguish a graded rise, a step, a peak below the top and a contender-driven dominant-high profile, yet these imply different mechanisms. Here the correlation-based classes misread every inverted-U profile. Even a high/middle/low split read the same contender peak as an inverted U, as dominant-high or as flat depending only on group size. Comparisons across species or populations that bin ranks this way can therefore disagree for that reason alone. Reporting load by rank position, with the alpha and the next two ranks separated (Levy et al. 2020), is more informative. Second, the same burden can be carried by different channels (deficit, defeat, intimidation, contest effort) depending on ecology. Measures of energetic state and of aggression given and received are needed alongside hormones to tell these apart, as recent work combining thyroid hormones and glucocorticoids in baboons illustrates (Gesquiere et al. 2025).

Limitations. The model is dimensionless and unfitted. Its outputs are qualitative predictions, not estimates for any species, and simulated parameter recovery would not be validation. Group sizes were 6–20. At \(N = 20\), closed groups at the main base point did not order, so the larger-group tests relied on fission–fusion or on lower choice noise, and the middle peak could not be tested there. Individuals are exchangeable by design, so phenotype-dependent costs lie outside the model. Load is a linear integral of activation; hormone dynamics, receptor regulation and feedback, which can make chronic challenge lower rather than raise glucocorticoids (Dickens and Romero 2013), are not represented. Hierarchies formed only with resource-holding feedback, a per-individual scalar. The shapes reported are therefore those of condition-mediated hierarchies, and structure depended on interactions among several parameters rather than on any one.

Within these limits, the model shows that self-organizing dominance can produce most of the rank–stress diversity seen in social animals. The patterns it cannot produce point to specific additional mechanisms that field studies can look for.
